items.leadSynopsis: The article describes how **Donald Trump’s decision to launch a military attack on Iran led to the death of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, but instead of quickly ending the conflict, it triggered a broader war, regional instability, and a global oil crisis.

items.biasAssessment: The article may contain some analytical bias because it focuses heavily on the negative consequences of the U.S. decision to attack Iran, such as the escalation of war, economic crisis, and lack of a clear strategy. He has already taken some military steps, such as sending thousands of Marines and military equipment to the region. The US is also targeting Iranian ships that lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Trump has suggested forming a group of countries to protect ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, which is a very important route for global oil. But if he does less, Iran could still threaten shipping and oil supplies. The war is also affecting the US economy. Gas prices have gone up, with the average price reaching about $3.72 per gallon. months, sending shockwaves through import-dependent economies like Japan.
The impact was severe. Japan relied on imports for nearly all its oil, and its postwar economic boom abruptly stalled. Panic buying spread and in 1974, Japan’s economy contracted for the first time since World War II, marking the start of slower growth.

items.articleTitle: Day 33 of Middle East conflict — Trump’s first address to the nation on Iran war
items.leadSynopsis: Trump’s address: President Donald Trump used familiar talking points in his first address to the nation on the Iran war, telling Americans the war is “nearing completion” and projected another two or three weeks of involvement. items.articleTitle: Trump makes his best case for the war — but fails to ease worries about how it will end
items.leadSynopsis: Trump say the war is end
items.actionWhat:
Donald Trump faced a high bar Wednesday night in his national address on Iran.

He appeared before a country that has not only lost confidence in his presidency, according to the latest polls, but that has soured on his new war and is profoundly worried about its impact on the economy.

Millions of people in the Middle East and across the world want to know when the war will end and how — or even if — he’ll fix its tumultuous aftermath, including Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which threatens a global recession.

items.articleTitle: Trump leaves key questions unanswered as he seeks to calm nerves over Iran war
items.leadSynopsis: President Donald Trump's address from the White House on Wednesday evening was - despite some speculation beforehand - largely a rehash of what he has been saying for days about the Iran war.
items.actionWhat:
- In a 20-minute primetime speech, he said the "core strategic objectives" of the US-Israeli military operation were "nearing completion" after a month of war and projected it would last another two to three weeks.
- There were the usual threats against Iran, too, including a repeated pledge to bomb the country "back to the stone age".
- Trump urged Americans to see this war as an "investment" in their future, and suggested it was nothing compared to other conflicts over the past century.
- But there was little here for those hoping for clear answers on where this war is heading or potential exit ramps for the US.
items.actionWhy:
- Polls suggest a consistent majority of voters disapprove of the military operation he launched on 28 February, so that Trump did attempt to persuade Americans of the merits of this war.
- Meanwhile, the average price of gas in the US has topped $4 for the first time in nearly four years and the president's approval ratings are cratering.
items.biasAssessment: - I think there is bias because the author uses loaded words such as 'rehash', 'glaring omissions', and 'casting about' to criticize President Trump's address.

items.actionWhat: - China joins Pakistan, which has emerged as an unlikely mediator in the US-Israel war against Iran. Officials in Beijing and Islamabad have presented a five-point plan with the aim of bringing about a ceasefire and re-opening the vital Strait of Hormuz.
items.actionWhy:
- The war in Iran leads to regional instability and China needs a stable global economy as it is heavily reliant on selling goods around the world as it tries to revive an ailing domestic economy.
- If the rest of the world begins to slow down economically because of an energy shock, that's going to be tough for China's factories and exporters.
items.biasAssessment: - I think there is bias because, after discussing China's efforts to play peacemaker, the author mentioned China's alignment with Russia, its increasing control of Hong Kong and its repeated threats to take self-governed Taiwan by force intended to undermine China's credibility.

The warring parties - Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) - are both accused of sexual violence. items.articleTitle: International law experts allege violations in Iran war
items.leadSynopsis: More than 100 international law experts have signed an open letter alleging that the US, Israel, and Iran are in "clear breach" of the UN Charter and fundamental humanitarian laws, citing "no quarter" rhetoric and mass civilian casualties.
items.actionActor: 100+ experts (including former US Army judges and Yale professors), Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and the UN's Tom Fletcher.
items.actionAffected: 1,606 civilians killed in Iran (244 children); 1,345 killed in Lebanon; 168 killed in a single strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab.
items.actionWhere: Minab (Southern Iran), Petah Tikva (Israel), Kuwait (refinery hit), and New York (Just Security journal).
items.actionWhat: Legal experts condemned Hegseth’s "no quarter" comments as "especially forbidden" and a potential war crime.
items.actionWhy: The experts argue the initial attack bypassed the UN Security Council and that "outdated intelligence" led to the reckless destruction of civilian infrastructure.
items.biasAssessment: The report contrasts the high-level legal testimony of the signatories with the White House's dismissive tone, framing the administration as "reckless" and showing a "disrespect for the rules" of war.

items.articleTitle: Oil prices jump and shares drop after Trump threatens more Iran strikes
items.leadSynopsis: Global markets reacted with "cynicism" to President Trump’s White House address, causing Brent crude to surge back to $109 after he failed to provide a concrete timeline for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

items.actionWhat: Trump urged other nations to "just take" the Strait themselves; analysts warned that infrastructure damage could take 3–5 years to repair.
items.actionWhy: Trump’s rhetoric lacked a specific resolution for energy flows; he claimed the Strait would open "naturally," but experts say a $2m-per-ship fee to use the waterway might become permanent.
items.biasAssessment: The report highlights a "reality check," contrasting the President’s optimistic view of a "natural" reopening with the grim technical reality of years of infrastructure repair and massive new transit fees.

items.actionWhat: Trump claimed Iran asked for a ceasefire (denied by Tehran); Israel struck a facility it claims produced chemical weapons; a new wave of Iranian projectiles was detected heading toward Israel.
items.actionWhy: Trump believes the primary goal—preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon—has been achieved; Pezeshkian demands "guarantees" against future aggression before any de-escalation.
items.biasAssessment: The report maintains a skeptical tone regarding Trump's "imminent end" claims, noting that he has made similar promises throughout the month while military strikes actually appear to be intensifying.

items.biasAssessment: The report is highly technical and objective, using flight-tracking data and satellite "matching" to confirm the loss of an asset that US Central Command has notably declined to comment on.

items.articleTitle: Iran war economic shocks will last 'months', says Australia's PM

Officials are also trying to increase fuel supply and imports. At the same time, people were advised to avoid panic buying and use less fuel, such as taking public transport instead of driving
items.actionWhy: The problem is caused by the larger conflict involving Iran, the US, and Israel, which has affected global oil supply. A key issue is the near-blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, where about 20% of the world’s oil passes through. Because less oil is moving through this important route, fuel prices have increased around the world, including in Australia. Even though Australia is not directly involved in the war, it still feels the effects through higher costs
items.biasAssessment: The article mainly reports facts and includes quotes from the Prime Minister. It explains both the problem and the government’s response clearly

items.leadSynopsis: US Army’s first new lethal grenade since the Vietnam War uses shock waves to kill
items.actionWhat:
The US Army last month introduced its first new lethal hand grenade since the Vietnam War, a plastic weapon that uses shock waves rather than shrapnel to kill enemies.

The new grenade, called the M111, becomes the Army’s choice for urban combat, when troops must clear indoor areas to take and hold territory, because there’s less risk of collateral damage.

It’s the first new grenade introduced for US forces since 1968, when the MK3A2 entered combat during the Vietnam War. That munition was withdrawn in the 1970s because it contains asbestos, tiny fibers of which can become lodged in the lungs leading to fatal diseases including cancer.

items.articleTitle: Trump allows Russian oil tanker to reach Cuba, breaking his fuel blockade of island
items.byline: By Danya Gainor , Chris Liu Chris Lau , Anna Chernova
items.leadSynopsis: Trump allows Russian oil tanker to reach Cuba, breaking his fuel blockade of island
items.actionWhat:
A Russian-flagged oil tanker reportedly reached Cuba on Monday after US President Donald Trump allowed it to break his administration’s fuel blockade of the island nation as its energy crisis deepens.

The Russian transport ministry said the Anatoly Kolodkin – a tanker with nearly 730,000 barrels of oil onboard – had arrived at the Matanzas port in Cuba on Monday, according to Russian state-run news agencies. CNN could not independently verify the ship’s location; data from the ship tracking site MarineTraffic showed it as being just off Cuba on Monday morning.

Dmitry Peskov, the spokesman for Russian President Vladimir Putin also said on Monday the ship had arrived in Cuba. Asked if the US agreed to let the tanker through, Peskov said: “As for the American side, I can only confirm that this issue was indeed raised in advance during contacts with our American counterparts.”

items.articleTitle: ‘Like relying on a drug dealer:’ The world’s dependence on oil and gas has exposed a dangerous vulnerability
items.byline: By Laura Povembernsion,NElla Nilsen Ella Nilsen
items.articleDateline: 3 hr ago PUBLISHED Apr 2, 2026, 4:00 AM ET
items.leadSynopsis:
The Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has shown how easy it is to for one country to turn geography into a ferocious weapon with devastating global impacts. It also reveals a truth about the dangers of a fossil fuel-powered global energy system: It’s heavily reliant on a handful of narrow maritime chokepoints, all in volatile regions.

The Strait is a narrow passage of deep, dark-blue water that tracks along Iran’s arid, mountainous southern coastline and transports round a fifth of world’s oil and gas.

The impacts of its effective closure have unfolded swiftly, sending energy prices soaring and shockwaves through the global economy. It’s led to fuel shortages and rationing and fears of a global recession.

But if the global energy system were powered primarily by wind, solar and batteries, rather than oil and gas, would a similar war trigger the same levels of disruption?

Experts say there’s a key difference between the two: Fossil fuels depend on continuous shipments of oil and gas; any disruption cuts off energy supply immediately. In contrast, clean energy supply chains are centered on the transportation of equipment — not the energy itself.

items.articleTitle: Is Trump's pause on attacking Iranian energy for diplomacy or an escalation?

items.actionWhat: The US paused planned strikes on Iranian energy targets. Analysts are divided on whether this move signals de-escalation and openness to talks or a tactical pause before further action. The decision has created uncertainty about the US strategy moving forward.
items.actionWhy: The US is balancing military pressure with diplomatic opportunities. Concerns about global oil supply, regional stability, and international reactions influence decision-making. The pause may be intended to create space for negotiations or reassess strategy.

items.articleTitle: Jeremy Bowen: Trump is waging war based on instinct and it isn't working
items.leadSynopsis: Veteran correspondent Jeremy Bowen analyzes how the lack of a "Plan B" has left the US stuck in an asymmetric war of attrition, with Iran using its geography to neutralize American military superiority.
items.actionActor: Donald Trump, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the legacy of Eisenhower’s military planning.
items.actionAffected: 1,464 Iranian civilians killed; Global oil supply (20% cut off); US Marine Expeditionary Units and the 82nd Airborne (on standby).
items.actionWhere: The Oval Office, Tehran, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Bab al-Mandab Strait (Red Sea).
items.actionWhat: Trump has twice postponed threats to destroy Iran’s power grid; the Houthis have resumed missile strikes on Israel; the US is considering risky amphibious landings on Kharg Island.
items.actionWhy: Trump expected a "Venezuela-style" quick win, but Iran’s regime is built on institutional and ideological resilience that survives the death of individual leaders.
items.biasAssessment: Bowen is sharply critical of Trump’s "bones-based" strategy, contrasting it with Netanyahu’s 40-year clarity and Eisenhower’s disciplined planning, ultimately warning that this war could be America's "Suez moment"—a turning point of imperial decline.

items.articleTitle: How Trump and the oil markets move in sync: a tango in five charts
items.byline: Jemma Crew, Tommy Lumby, and Natalie Sherman
items.leadSynopsis: One month into the conflict, the "Trump Effect" on oil markets is weakening as investors grow skeptical of his claims regarding peace talks, leaving Brent crude sitting at a volatile $112 a barrel.
items.actionActor: President Donald Trump, global oil traders, and investment analysts (Quilter Cheviot, AJ Bell).
items.actionAffected: Global energy prices (up from $72 to $112); US stock markets (largest drop of the war on Thursday).
items.actionWhere: Global markets and the Strait of Hormuz.
items.actionWhat: Trump announced a delay in strikes on Iranian energy until April 6, claiming talks were going "very well"; markets largely ignored the reassurance, with oil prices continuing to rise.
items.actionWhy: A "huge gap" exists between Trump’s optimism and Tehran’s silence, leading investors to believe the rhetoric is aimed at moving prices rather than actual policy.
items.biasAssessment: The report frames the President as a "skittish" communicator whose credibility is becoming a "casualty of war," contrasting his social media tactics with the "downright cynicism" now felt by professional investors.

items.articleTitle: Three charts that are warning signs flashing for Trump on Iran war
items.byline: Anthony Zurcher, reporting from CPAC in Dallas
items.leadSynopsis: New polling data shows President Trump’s approval rating has sagged to 40% as the Iran war drives petrol prices toward $4 a gallon, threatening a Republican "undoing" in the November midterm elections.
items.actionActor: President Donald Trump, Ipsos/Pew Research (pollsters), and independent voters.
items.actionAffected: Trump’s economic approval (dropped to 29%, lower than Joe Biden’s lowest mark); Petrol prices (averaging near $4/gallon); 2026 Midterm election candidates.
items.actionWhere: Dallas, Texas (CPAC) and across the United States.
items.actionWhat: Democrats outperformed Republicans by 13% in 2025 special elections; independent voters are turning against the military intervention.
items.actionWhy: Ongoing dissatisfaction with the cost of living and "economic anxiety" exacerbated by the war’s disruption of global oil.
items.biasAssessment: The report uses data to highlight a "dangerous territory" for the President, contrasting the defiant "pay the price" attitude of his base at CPAC with the broader public's growing opposition to the "war of choice."

items.articleTitle: Trump is waging war based on instinct and it isn't working
items.leadSynopsis: Some old truths about warfare have been knocking on the door of the Oval Office in the month since US President Donald Trump and Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent US and Israeli warplanes to bomb Iran.
items.actionActor: Donal Trump and Israel's prime minister
items.actionWhat: Some old truths about Trump and Israel’s Prime minister appeared since they sent airplanes to bomb Iran. Oval office thought that is an old warfare.
items.actionWhy: Because they keep the old warfare from World War II.
items.biasAssessment: No because the news talks from multiple perspectives : Trump's end point; Iran's obduracy.

items.articleTitle: Iran war splits older and younger conservatives - as pressure builds for Trump to find exit ramp
items.byline: Anthony Zurcher -North America correspondent, reporting from CPAC in Dallas
items.leadSynopsis: A majority of the American public, polls suggest, have been against the ongoing US-Israeli military campaign in Iran from the day it started.
items.actionWhat: American people and some members of US government have been worried about Iran war. They don’t think it is good for US.
items.actionWhy: Because Iran war had stepped to fourth week
items.biasAssessment: No because there are multiple perspective.

items.articleTitle: UN human rights chief calls on US to conclude probe into Iran school strike
items.leadSynopsis: The UN's human rights chief has urged the US to conclude its investigation and publish its findings into a deadly strike on an Iranian primary school that happened on the first day of the war last month.
items.actionWhat: The UN's human rights chief urged US to conclude deadly strikes to a primary school in Iran. There were at least 168 people died - according Iran official.
items.actionWhy: Because Iran had been in a war with Israel and US.
items.biasAssessment: No, because there are opinion of some civilians.

items.actionWhat: Iran war splits older and younger conservatives - as pressure builds for Trump to find exit ramp
items.actionWhy: At the annual Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Texas, some of the party faithful expressed concern about why the US started this war, how Donald Trump is going to end it and whether the effort has been worth the costs.
